newsitem.title: USA: The skinny on diet books -- factual or full of baloney.
newsitem.headline: The skinny on diet books -- factual or full of baloney.

text.p: Almost everyone either wants to go on a diet, is on a diet, or is recovering from a diet. Just look at the streams of new diet books that come on the market at the rate of one or more a month.
From medical doctors to diet gurus to the stars, there are dozens of diet books available. Some books give reasonable advice, others can be downright dangerous.
How does a person decide if one method of shedding love handles is better than another? How does one select the best book with a safe, healthy diet, espcially with so many to choose from?
There are no simple answers, but if the book's diet plan sounds illogical, chances are it is.

A good rule of thumb is to look for books that promote a balanced diet, do not restrict specific types of foods (such as dairy, carbohydrates or protein), can be tailored to fit your particular lifestyle and include foods you like to eat, said Elaine Turner, assistant professor of food science and human nutrition at the University of Florida in Gainesville.
"Look for approaches to weight loss that focus on long-term eating habits, not 10-day or 30-day programs" -- what Turner called "the weight loss flavor of the month."

"Forget quick weight loss schemes," agreed Delia Hammock, Good Housekeeping Institute's associate director and resident nutritionist. "If a programme or book promises more than one or two pounds a week, it's a bad diet," she said.
"Everybody wants a magic solution... everyone wants to know, 'how can I loose weight fast?'"

The bottom line is -- you can't, Hammock said. And any diet book that says you can is promoting an unhealthy plan. In any diet, the slower the weight comes off, the more likely it is to stay off, she said.

"Calories are the bottom line. Cutting your fat can help simply because fat is a very condensed food. Fat doesn't fill you up" and contains far more calories per gram than either carbohydrates or protein.
The diet books that promise to turn back the hands of time and gravity are to be avoided as well.

In addition, avoid diet books where the calorie intake is too low, such as below 1,000 calories a day. "Low caloric intake slows down the metabolism too much," Hammock said, making it almost impossible to keep the weight off long term.
In addition to a balanced diet, Turner said, "any sensible long-term approach to weight control has to incorporate more physical activity."
Some diet books, particularly those "written" by celebrities, may give readers false hope about how much weight they can loose.

By losing 10 percent of one's body weight, which may be plenty for some or just the tip of the iceberg for others, a person can lower their blood pressure and generally improve their well-being, Hammock said.
"Improving health is the most important, not fitting into size six jeans," Hammock said. "I don't believe in diets. I believe in healthy eating. It's a plan for the rest of your life."
Hammock looked at more than 30 popular diet books. Here's a short list of the good, the bad and the ugly.

She gives two thumbs up to: "Weigh Less, Live Longer" (John Wiley & Sons, 1996) by Dr. Louis Aronne. It is "a useful volume to start you on healthier eating habits," she wrote in the June edition of Good Housekeeping magazine.
Another "two thumbs up" entry is "Eating Thin For Life" (Chapters Publishing Ltd., 1997) by Anne Fletcher, which is "ideal for those who are serious about changing their eating habits."
Given one thumb up is: "The New Hilton Head Metabolism Diet" (Warner Books, 1996) by Peter Miller. "Those who prefer a structured regimin may like this plan," Hammock writes.
One thumb down goes to: "Suzanne Somers' Eat Great, Lose Weight (Crown Publishers, 1996) by Suzanne Somers -- "a mishmash of nonsensical rules";
"Mastering the Zone" (Regan Books, 1997) by Barry Sears. "This complex, restrictive plan's claims...are not supported by scientific evidence";

"The Carbohydrate Addict's LifeSpan Program" (Dutton, 1997) by Richard Heller and Rachael Heller -- "daily intake for three sample menus averaged almost 2,000 calories", what is needed to maintain weight, not lose it;
"Fitonics for Life" (Avon Books,1996) by Marilyn Diamond and Donald Burton Schnell -- "the theories behind this diet with all its hoo-ha about enzymes are only good for laughs;"
"The 5 Day Miracle Diet" (Ballantine Books, 1996) by Adele Puhm. "There is no miracle here -- just a crash diet."
Two thumbs down goes to: "Dr. Atkins' New Diet Revolution" (Avon Books, 1992) by Dr. Robert Atkins. "This unbalanced, high-fat diet is neither new nor a revolution;"
"The New Beverly Hills Diet" (Health Communications, 1996), by Judy Mazel. "Stay away: It's a potential health hazard;"
"Eat Right 4 Your Body Type (Putnam's Sons, 1996), by Peter D'Adamo. "There is very little scientific evidence to back up D'Adamo's unusual theories abut diet and blood type."
